title: The Many and the Few
deck:
A reply to questions left scribbled in the margins—about division, democracy, and the forces that keep the many from standing together.
Perhaps freedom begins not with becoming the same, but with learning to stand together without demanding sameness.
author: Muhammad Aizaz Ahmad - Editor S&S
body:
It is with deep respect for you, and for the entirety of your soul, that I write to you about your health and serenity. May both be at their very best. And yes, I am well too, in a lively condition.
The purpose of writing to you after such a long time is not to remind you of the regrets, the pain, or the moments we once shared and lost. Rather, it is an invitation—an attempt to revisit the questions you once scribbled in the margins of
When the People Claimed the Right to Rule Over Themselves.

In the marginalia, you had asked why we, as the people of a united nation, are somehow divided into various factions—be they religious, political, racial, or romantic, the latter being a rather generalised category. I feel obliged to answer them all, though I shall leave the romantic divisions untouched, owing to their fragility.
So, we, the people of this “united nation,” stand divided, yet have somehow adopted the constitution of democracy—which itself is built upon rather muddy waters—in our attempt to place ourselves among the nations that claim a higher moral standing than oligarchies and monarchies.
But therein lies an announced sin.
The very oligarchies and monarchies that we, as a democratically united country, condemn are institutions before which we still prostrate ourselves behind dark curtains.
Were I to descend too deeply into this hypocrisy of our democracy, I would fail to answer the question you left for me to contemplate. So I shall leave it aside, though not entirely.
Division, historically, has been a tool of the very few against the many. And the few have often outmanoeuvred the many—not through untamed power, but through their ability to corrode trust.
In doing so, religion, political doctrine, and racial segregation have repeatedly proved vital instruments.
Yet something within us continues to resist this decay.
Perhaps that resistance is what may still grant us the true sense of freedom and individual empowerment—things we seem to lack at this very moment.
We can thrive only when we learn to look beyond the mirror of religion, sect, and creed; beyond those reflections of ourselves that persuade us that difference must necessarily mean division.
Perhaps then we may achieve what the great powers of the past and present have always desired, yet so rarely managed to preserve: a people capable of standing together without first demanding that they become the same.
Until then, I wish you the softest night and the bravest day.
